summary: Comments on RFC 580. The author supports requiring machine-readable protocol documents but objects to preferring NLS files, since many sites have no way to convert their own text into NLS.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 582 supports sharing protocol documents in machine-readable form but objects to preferring NLS files. The author asks for a documented converter so sites can prepare documents with their existing tools.

subtitle: A request for a general way to convert formatted text into NLS files.

tldr.problem: RFC 580 preferred machine-readable protocol documents as NLS files, but many sites lacked a way to convert documents into that format.
tldr.mechanism: R. Clements supports machine-readable documents but asks for a generally available and predictable converter from formatted text to NLS.
tldr.outcome: RFC 582 is a comment on RFC 580 and updates it; the author suggests the Journal mail-receiving program might serve as the converter if it were documented and publicized.

today: The unit records RFC 582's status as Unknown and says it updates RFC 580. It is a comment about document formats and conversion to NLS.

sections.title: Support for Machine-Readable Documents
sections.content:
R. Clements says he fully supports requiring protocol documents to be machine-readable. He notes that, in his situation, a line printer is more reliable than a copying machine.

His objection is specifically to RFC 580's preference for NLS files. He says the problem is the lack of conversion mechanisms into NLS, not NLS itself or the process of retrieving files.
sections.plainLanguage: The author agrees that protocol documents should be available as computer files. He objects to choosing NLS as the preferred format when sites cannot easily create it.

sections.title: Let Sites Use Their Existing Tools
sections.content:
Most sites have their own text editors and RUNOFF programs or equivalents. The RFC notes that large protocol documents are often prepared at least partly with secretarial help, and argues that people should be able to use familiar tools on their home system.

Clements therefore proposes a general program for converting nicely formatted text into NLS files. He says the converter should at least be generally available and predictable.
sections.plainLanguage: Writers should be able to prepare documents with the tools they already know. A shared converter could then produce the NLS files needed by the NIC.

sections.title: Possible Journal Converter
sections.content:
The author suggests that the program receiving mail for the Journal might already perform the needed conversion. He does not claim that it does; he says that if it can, it needs more documentation than the mail-focused description in RFC 543.

He also asks that the converter's existence and use be publicized so sites can find and use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The Journal's mail program might be able to convert files, but the author is unsure. If it can, people need clear instructions and notice that it exists.

references.text: RFC 580, the document being commented on.
